nameStory: The name 'jagged chickweed' comes from its small, serrated or 'jagged' leaves that distinguish it from other smooth-leaved chickweeds. Like other chickweeds, it was historically considered good food for chickens and small birds, who would eagerly peck at its tender leaves and seeds.
description: Jagged chickweed is a small, delicate annual plant that forms low mats or upright clumps reaching just 2-6 inches tall. This European native has tiny white flowers arranged in small umbrella-like clusters and narrow, pointed leaves with slightly toothed edges. It's a spring ephemeral that completes its entire life cycle quickly, often appearing and disappearing before many people notice it in early spring.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow leaves with slightly jagged or serrated edges that feel rough when rubbed between your fingers, unlike the smooth leaves of common chickweed

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with 5 deeply notched petals arranged in small umbrella-shaped clusters at the stem tips, giving them a delicate, lacy appearance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small patches or individual plants that stay very low to the ground, rarely exceeding 6 inches in height with multiple thin, slightly sticky stems

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, urn-shaped seed capsules that split open to reveal tiny brown seeds, often with the empty capsules persisting after seeds disperse

habitat: Look for jagged chickweed in disturbed soils, along path edges, in gardens, and waste areas where the ground has been recently turned or is somewhat sandy. It prefers open, sunny spots with well-drained soil and is often found in areas with other small weedy plants.

seasonality.spring: This is prime time for jagged chickweed - look for the tiny white flowers blooming from March through May, with the plant completing most of its growth during cool spring weather.
seasonality.summer: Plants have usually finished flowering and set seed by early summer, with dried seed capsules often the only remaining evidence of their presence.
seasonality.fall: Seeds germinate in fall, forming small rosettes of jagged leaves that will overwinter and bloom the following spring.
seasonality.winter: Small leaf rosettes may be visible in milder winters, pressed close to the ground and often taking on reddish tones in cold weather.

funFact: Despite being called a chickweed, jagged chickweed is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only 5 times by naturalists - making it one of the most elusive members of the pink family and a true treasure for any plant enthusiast lucky enough to find it!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common chickweed, but jagged chickweed's serrated leaf edges and umbrella-like flower clusters set it apart from common chickweed's smooth leaves and scattered individual flowers. Memory trick: 'Jagged' leaves for jagged chickweed, smooth leaves for common chickweed.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'chickweed' applies to several different plant species that aren't all closely related - jagged chickweed is in the pink family, while some other 'chickweeds' belong to entirely different plant families, which can cause confusion for beginning botanists.
compareHints: Jagged chickweed is the only species in its genus (Holosteum) found in New England, making it unique among local plants. Within the pink family, it's distinguished from other small white-flowered relatives like pearlworts and sandworts by its distinctive umbrella-shaped flower clusters and jagged leaf margins. Most other pink family members in our region have either smooth-edged leaves or very different flower arrangements.
